2. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Several guest stars were considered for recurring roles on Cheers, including Kirstie Alley and Bernadette Birkett.
3. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley played Rebecca Howe for six seasons after Shelley Long left the show.
4. [ASSISTANT_SAID] George Wendt's real-life wife, Bernadette Birkett, played Norm's wife, Vera, in several episodes.
5. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Other guest stars who appeared in multiple episodes include John Mahoney, Emma Thompson, Bebe Neuwirth, and Jay Thomas.
6. [USER] User was surprised to learn that Kirstie Alley was originally a guest star on Cheers.
7. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley joined the cast of Cheers in season 6 after Shelley Long left the show.
8. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley played the character Rebecca Howe, who was initially hired as the manager of Cheers by Sam Malone.
9. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley's performance was well-received by audiences and critics.
10. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley won an Emmy Award for her role in 1991.
11. [USER] User finds it fascinating to learn about the behind-the-scenes of a TV show.
12. [USER] User inquired about interesting facts about the Cheers set.
13. [ASSISTANT_SAID] The "Cheers" sign that hung outside the bar was a real sign from a neighborhood bar in Boston.
14. [ASSISTANT_SAID] The iconic Cheers bar was built on a soundstage in Hollywood, not in Boston.
15. [ASSISTANT_SAID] The bar was designed after a real Boston bar, the Bull & Finch Pub, which still exists today.
16. [ASSISTANT_SAID] The set included a replica of the famous Cheers pool table, designed to look like a pool table from the 1890s.
17. [ASSISTANT_SAID] Fans would often write letters to the fictional Cheers bar, thinking it was a real place.
18. [ASSISTANT_SAID] The front door of the bar was intentionally squeaky for comedic timing during the show's dialogue.
19. [ASSISTANT_SAID] A "walk-and-talk" section of the bar was created so characters could move through the set while talking.
20. [ASSISTANT_SAID] The studio audience set was built above the main set, allowing for a bird's-eye view of the action.
